Voice AI is ready to talk to customers. The harder question is: how would you know it is safe, helpful and worth the cost? This is what we found when we put it to the test.

We built an independent test environment, a simulated bank and simulated customers, and ran five selected external prototype services through it: OpenAI GPT-Realtime, Google Gemini Live, xAI Grok Voice, ElevenLabs Agents and Amazon Nova Sonic. These were tested outside of work. A sixth service, OpenAI's GPT-Live, was tested in follow-up scenarios, but its main-run results come from an earlier prompt, so it is not in this comparison. In total: forty customer situations, repeated three times each, six hundred recorded runs.

Every service faced the same situations, the same bank and the same scoring rules. Controls sit outside the service, holding speech back until policy allows it, and every run is written to a tamper-evident evidence ledger. If evidence is missing, that counts against the result. It is never quietly treated as a pass.

The first finding is protection. In six hundred runs, no service carried out a prohibited action. That is the result of the services and the controls working together. It does not mean every check passed, and the report records the failures too.

The second finding is that getting the job done varied. When a customer asked the bank to do something, xAI and ElevenLabs completed all thirty-six eligible requests. Gemini and GPT-Realtime completed thirty-five, and Nova twenty-nine.

Saying the right thing held up. Every service passed all of the spoken-fact checks that could be decided, such as amounts and dates. Overall quality scored between ninety-seven point six and ninety-nine point six percent, and the statistics cannot separate the services, so there is no clear overall winner.

Cost varied the most. The median voice cost per priced run ran from four tenths of a cent, for Gemini, to three point three cents, for xAI. That is roughly an eight times spread, for services that scored close together on quality. This covers voice usage only.

A small follow-up tested a caller who asks for a person, and then asks again. Four services transferred every time. Nova did so five times in nine, and GPT-Live never did, offering to help with the account instead. In a separate cancellation check, five services completed a confirmed cancellation every time, while Nova verified the caller but did not cancel, for a reason we have not established. These are small runs, outside the scores, but they are a reminder that handing over to a person needs testing too.

Two lessons stood out. First, a reply that sounds successful is not proof the bank action actually happened, so the test checks the action itself. Second, broad prompt tuning moved individual results but not the overall ranking, while a couple of targeted prompt lines fixed specific failures, like Nova's handover to a person.

What this does not tell you matters. The callers are scripted, clear and synthetic. Samples are small. This is not a prediction of customer outcomes, not a certification, and it has not yet measured the services you already run, such as Amazon Connect or our internal agentic platforms. It is evidence about specific prototype configurations, on a specific day.

So what? Services that look the same on quality can differ sharply on completion and cost, and none of this shows up in a demo. The next step is to bring the harness inside the work environment, and baseline what we already run, Amazon Connect and our internal agentic platforms, against these prototypes. Pick the customer journey where a missed request or an unsafe action would hurt most. Define what helpful, protected and understandable mean for it. Then compare real experiences, on the same evidence, before anything new speaks to a customer.
